characterList.description: Middle-aged, with graying hair and a beard, wearing a white shirt and glasses.
characterList.name: Man

content_metadata.description: An engaging and informative showcase of the vintage Bell and Howell 414 PD Zoomatic Director Series 8mm Movie Camera, featuring detailed demonstrations and historical context.

qAndA.answer: The camera has a 3-to-1 'Varamat' zoom lens with a range of 9 to 27 millimeters.
qAndA.question: What type of lens does the camera have?

qAndA.answer: He used Agfachrome 200D, an E6 process slide film.
qAndA.question: What film stock did the man use to shoot the footage shown at the end of the video?

qAndA.answer: He forgot to bring neutral density filters, and the location he was shooting at was very bright.
qAndA.question: Why did the man have to use his sunglasses over the camera lens?

qAndA.answer: It's the same model that Abraham Zapruder used to capture the assassination of President Kennedy.
qAndA.question: What makes this specific camera model historically significant?

qAndA.answer: It has three prongs. This prevents the film from being loaded incorrectly with the emulsion facing the wrong way.
qAndA.question: How many 'prongs' does the take-up spool have, and why is that relevant?

activities.description: Introduces the Bell and Howell 414 PD Zoomatic Director Series camera.
Demonstrates the camera's features, including the clockwork motor, wind indicator, film speed settings, and zoom lens.
Discusses the camera's exposure settings, the 3-to-1 zoom range, and its historical significance.
Talks about his experience shooting with the camera, including the film stock used, the brightness of the location, and the need for neutral density filters.
Mentions the film stock options available for the camera and recommends Spectra Film and Video in Hollywood, California.

activities.description: Shows a roll of Kodachrome film that he processed in black and white, explaining how the 8mm film works.
Demonstrates how to load the film into the camera using the take-up spool and explains how the mechanism prevents the emulsion from facing the wrong way.
Discusses the 'P' and 'D' designations in the camera's model number, explaining the power zoom feature and the dual selenium meters.
Mentions the camera's age and where it was sold, and expresses his interest in shooting more black and white film with it.

Off of this clockwork motor has a wind indicator. You can't overwind it.
And then the normal speed 16 frames per second. Slow motion runs at 48 frames per second.
At normal speed, each frame is exposed for about 135th of a second.
And if you're running at 48 frames per second, it's about 1 1 100th of a second per frame.
It has what they call the 3-to-1 Veramatt Zune. It's 9 to 27mm.
Like a lot of these because the back of the lens is really near the film gate.
It's pretty easy to get them really bright. This one is F1.8 to F22.
It's a nice lens. It's 11 elements. And yes, it's that camera.
This is the exact same model that Abraham's a pruder used to capture the assassination of President Kennedy.
I think a little bit sick that I got it, but I am shooting with it.
The camera only goes normally to ISO 40.
The film that I was able to get was ISO 200. I was shooting at the salt and sea.
It's really, really bright there. I forgot to take neutral density filters.
So I used my polarizing sunglasses over the lens.
And that was good for about two stops.
So once you get past the film, you can manually set your F-stop.
So shooting at about ISO 50 with the glasses in front of it at F22, I was able to get some usable footage.
I used Agfacrome 200D. It's an E6 process slide film.

But you can see that on these old 8mm cameras, it's really 16mm film perforated on both sides.

and you end up with the 8mm film with the sprocket holes along one side.
